docs.text: Book Recommendations Skill The skill The rubric The changelog This skill recommends romance novels. It filters out particular categories (novellas, mafia/vampire/demon/alien characters, anyone under 18, YA), excludes a list of specific authors I dislike, enforces a strict output format with content warnings, and does not announce what it filtered out. The Problem Before I built the skill, Claude was giving me recommendations of authors I disliked, repeating authors in the list, and including books I had read already. Often there were not enough recommendations so I had to keep editing my prompt to Claude. What I Built It only gives me recommendations I have not read, in my preferred format, in groups of 15 at a time. Screenshots Here is what that looks like: How I Built It I created the written skill in VS Code and tested it with Claude Code. Challenges In the first round of testing, I had two instruction defects. First, a missing closing "---" that would have broken the file. Second, a sentence that contradicted itself (it said no children but also allowed for children in the epilogue). In the second round, I had a progressive disclosure issue. The list of books I did not want recommended was huge and would make the skill too long to read easily. I created the already-read.md file so I had a separate place to store past titles. In the third round, I found a state-persistence limitation in the model. Results still included books I had read that I had not added to already-read.md initially. I edited the skill to add all recommendations to the "do not recommend" list after recommending them. Future Improvements I am still considering whether the summary is necessary, and if it should be shortened.

docs.text: Eval notes Rubric defect: unverifiable is not pass Found during Run 1. The problem: The rubric only has pass and fail, so a criterion nobody can check resolves to pass by default. That means it reports "verified compliant" when the truth is "no contradicting evidence found. Which criteria are affected: 9 and 10. Both need the book text; review sites don't carry heat level or precise content-warning detail. Why it matters: A rubric that can't say "unknown" will report clean runs forever and stop being useful. How I'd close it: I want all criterion to be used so I added unverifiable as a permanent third outcome that's counted separately.

docs.text: Rubric Grading outcomes Each criterion is graded pass , fail , or unverifiable . Pass — positive evidence the criterion is met. Fail — positive evidence the criterion is violated. Unverifiable — the evidence needed to decide is not available from the sources used. Not a pass. Every unverifiable grade must name the entry, the missing evidence, and what would settle it. Unverifiable is counted separately in results and never folded into the pass count. If any entry in a criterion is unverifiable, the whole criterion is graded unverifiable. Minimum 15 books returned Pass: 15+ books, or explanation why fewer Fail: Fewer than 15 with no explanation Books and authors must be real and correctly attributed Pass: All books exist, have the correct title and author, and all authors are real Fail: Any book does not exist, has the wrong author, or any author does not exist Main character has no pregnancy or child before the epilogue Pass: Main characters are not parents or guardians of a child during the book and no main character is pregnant before the epilogue; an epilogue baby or pregnancy is optional Fail: A main character has a child, is a guardian of a child, or is pregnant at any point before the epilogue No books or authors from already-read.md Pass: None of the books or authors from already-read.md appear in the results Fail: Any book or author from already-read.md appears in the results No books or authors from the "skip all books by these authors" list Source of truth: this list is not defined in SKILL.md — it's the "## skip all books by these authors" section of already-read.md (currently /Users/nellgram/.claude/private-notes/book-recommendations/already-read.md ). Grade against that section, not against SKILL.md. Pass: None of the books or authors from the skip list appear in the results Fail: Any book or author from the skip list appears in the results No author appears twice within one set of results Pass: No author appears more than once in the same set of results Fail: Any author appears more than once in the same set of results No novellas Pass: Every recommended title is a full-length novel Fail: Any recommended title is a novella No prohibited main-character types Pass: No main character is a criminal, mafia member, vampire, demon, alien, or serial killer Fail: Any main character is one of the above Content warnings follow the required format and coverage Pass: Every entry with rape, torture, murder, cheating, BDSM, cancer, a main character's dog dying, or a main character with PTSD/other mental illness includes a content-warning line naming it; entries with none of those omit the line entirely; any rape/sexual-assault warning uses the format TYPE (ROLE, TIMING) with TYPE = "rape" or "sexual assault (not rape)", ROLE = "main character" or "secondary character", TIMING = "on page" or "past"; rape, torture, and murder are only present when not committed by a main character Fail: A qualifying content warning is missing, a content-warning line appears with nothing to warn about, a sexual-violence warning doesn't match the required format, or a main character commits rape, torture, or murder Unverifiable: Review-site summaries mention potentially qualifying content but don't confirm whether it occurs, who it happens to, or whether it's on page. Settled by: the book text. Closed-door/open-door heat level noted correctly Pass: A closed-door book includes a "Heat level: Closed door." line; an open-door book includes no heat-level line at all Fail: An open-door book includes a heat-level line, or a closed-door book has no heat-level line Unverifiable: No source consulted states whether the book is open or closed door. Settled by: the book text, or a review that explicitly names heat level. Every recommendation includes a link Pass: Every book entry includes a link to the title Fail: Any entry has no link Exclusion process kept invisible Pass: The response never mentions already-read.md, the skip-authors list, or why a specific book/author was excluded Fail: The response references the exclusion list, already-read status, or explains that something was skipped

If the scene involves physical contact, the entry is missing a sexual assault (not rape) (main character, on page/past) line and this criterion would fail for that entry. The Bodyguard (Katherine Center): one source flagged "suicidal ideation" among the book's content but didn't identify which character it belongs to (Hannah's mother's backstory is the likelier candidate, per other sources' framing of that same backstory). The run omitted a mental-illness warning on the assumption it isn't the main character's. Unconfirmed from primary text. No other entry showed evidence of an uncovered required topic (rape, torture, murder, cheating, BDSM, cancer, MC's dog dying) or a misformatted warning. Criterion 10 (heat level correctness): unverifiable (1 of 15 entries) — The Matchmaker's List (Sonya Lalli): no source found confirmed this as open- or closed-door; the run left off a heat-level line (defaulting to open-door), which is unverified either way. Criterion 11 (every entry has a link): pass — all 15 entries link to a real page for the title (Goodreads for 14; romance.io for The Spanish Love Deception , since no Goodreads URL was confirmed for it during the run). Criterion 12 (exclusion process invisible): pass — the response never mentions already-read.md, the skip-authors list, or why any book/author was excluded. Overall: 10 pass, 0 fail, 2 unverifiable (of 12 criteria). Unverifiable = criteria 9 and 10. Both need the book text; review-site summaries can't settle them.

docs.text: How to Read Your Explanation of Benefits (EOB) What Is an EOB? An Explanation of Benefits (EOB) is a document your health insurance company sends after you receive medical care. It is not a bill. It shows what your doctor charged, what your insurance paid, and what you may owe. What This Guide Covers This guide explains each section of your EOB so you know exactly what you are looking at. Your Personal Information At the top of your EOB you will find your name, address, member ID, and insurance group number. Check that this information is correct. The Four Key Numbers Every EOB shows four numbers that explain how your medical costs are shared between you and your insurance company. Billed Amount The total your doctor or provider charged for the service. Allowed Amount The amount your insurance company agrees to pay for the service based on your plan. This is usually less than the billed amount. Insurance Payment The portion of the allowed amount that your insurance paid directly to your provider. Amount You Owe What you must pay after your insurance pays its share. This may include your deductible, copay, or coinsurance. In-Network and Out-of-Network Costs Your costs depend on whether your provider is in your insurance network. In-network providers have agreements with your insurance company. Find the "network savings" box on your EOB to see how much you saved by using an in-network provider. Out-of-network providers do not have agreements with your insurance company. You may owe more than expected. Check the network savings line. If it shows $0, you used an out-of-network provider. Remark Codes Remark codes are short notes from your insurance company. They appear as 2 or 3 letters or numbers and explain details about your costs, such as why a service was partially paid or denied. Find the description of each code at the bottom of your EOB. How to Read Your Explanation of Benefits (EOB)

docs.text: An Explanation of Benefits (EOB) is a document your health insurance company sends after you receive medical care. It is not a bill. It shows what your doctor charged, what your insurance paid, and what you may owe.
docs.title: What Is an EOB?

docs.text: This guide explains each section of your EOB so you know exactly what you are looking at.
docs.title: What This Guide Covers

docs.text: At the top of your EOB you will find your name, address, member ID, and insurance group number. Check that this information is correct.
docs.title: Your Personal Information

docs.text: Every EOB shows four numbers that explain how your medical costs are shared between you and your insurance company.
docs.title: The Four Key Numbers

docs.text: The total your doctor or provider charged for the service.
docs.title: Billed Amount

docs.text: The amount your insurance company agrees to pay for the service based on your plan. This is usually less than the billed amount.
docs.title: Allowed Amount

docs.text: The portion of the allowed amount that your insurance paid directly to your provider.
docs.title: Insurance Payment

docs.text: What you must pay after your insurance pays its share. This may include your deductible, copay, or coinsurance.
docs.title: Amount You Owe

docs.text: Your costs depend on whether your provider is in your insurance network. In-network providers have agreements with your insurance company. Find the "network savings" box on your EOB to see how much you saved by using an in-network provider. Out-of-network providers do not have agreements with your insurance company. You may owe more than expected. Check the network savings line. If it shows $0, you used an out-of-network provider.

Content strategy Organization: The article follows agent workflows, moving from frequent tasks like renewals to less common situations such as lost cards or damaged materials, enabling quick reference. Scripted responses: The article includes templated answers and prepared responses that staff can use as starting points when communicating with patrons, similar to resources created for Google support teams. docs.text: Release Notes eReader App Monthly Updates View sample About Sample release notes were created for a fictional eReader application, drawing inspiration from Google Play's release note style. Reference: Release notes for Google Play Games on PC My approach Rather than presenting technical details, these notes spotlight practical user advantages. The strategy reduces support inquiries while promoting feature adoption. Key elements User value first: Focus on what users gain from updates — for instance, "Adds a streak tracker that shows how many days you've read in a row," instead of purely technical descriptions Action-oriented language: Descriptions enable users to understand how to leverage updated features Balanced scope: Mix of major features with performance improvements to establish realistic user expectations
